title: Interleaved Stream Scheduling Playbook
content:
Purpose
This playbook captures a concrete, operational approach for interleaving prefill and decode work across heterogeneous streams with differing priorities and latency profiles. It is meant to be an actionable design-to-implementation checklist for runtime engineers and SREs to reduce tail latency without sacrificing throughput and to make KV cache residency predictable.

Context and constraints
- Our runtime supports: continuous batching, pooled slots, per-request priority tags, and a shared KV cache with time-to-live semantics per model.
- Work types: prefill (longer compute, builds KV slices) and decode (fast sequential emits using cached KV).
- Goals: respect per-request latency SLO tiers (SLO: p99<=80ms for interactive tier; p99<=400ms for background), maintain high GPU utilization, and avoid priority inversion that starves interactive streams.
- Constraints: slot count limited by GPU memory, microbatch sizes affect kernel footprint and KV residency, and aggressive prefetching can evict KV entries used by low-latency streams.

Key concepts and vocabulary used in this doc
- Quantum: the minimum time-slice unit allocated to a stream slot (e.g., 2ms) for interleaving.
- Lease: a transient ownership of a compute slot for N consecutive quanta.
- Soft-priority: relative priority score (0-255) derived from customer tier + request-level hints.
- Priority-age: small additive boost to priority for requests waiting > X ms to prevent starvation (decay-based).
- Coalesced-prefetch token: a permission token allowing a prefill to touch multiple KV keys in a single batched kernel to reduce PCIe/host synchronizations.
- KV-residency budget: per-GPU soft accounting of bytes allocated to hot KV entries for a model or cohort.

High-level strategy
1) Time-slice interleaving with lease handoff: allocate slots in short quanta so short decodes can interleave between prefill kernels. Long prefill kernels take leases of limited length and are forced to yield at quantum boundaries when higher-priority decodes are pending.
2) Predictive microbatch shaping: prefer microbatches that match workload-sequence-length histograms per route; avoid blindly increasing microbatch size for throughput if it causes prefill kernels to monopolize slot time.
3) KV budget & pinning: maintain per-cohort KV residency budgets; allow priority cohorts to pin a small fraction of KV pages (immutable shards) to guarantee low-latency decodes do not get cache-missed.
4) Cooperative prefetch tokens: require prefill work to acquire a coalesced-prefetch token when touching >M keys so we can schedule such prefetches into low-latency windows.
5) Priority aging to avoid inversion: increment priority-age for requests waiting beyond threshold; cap age boost to prevent priority storms.

Detailed components and algorithms
A. Scheduling quantum and lease mechanics\- Quantum length: pick a base of 1.5–3 ms (start with 2 ms for experiments). This is a tradeoff: smaller quantum reduces tail for short decodes but increases context-switch overhead.\- Lease length: allow prefill kernels to request 1–K quanta (K tunable, default K=8). If a higher-priority decode arrives, the scheduler will preempt at the next quantum boundary unless the prefill holds a "nonpreemptible critical" flag (reserved for checkpoint flushes).\- Context switch cost accounting: measure empirical kernel teardown/setup cost in ms per model/kern; if switch cost > quantum, the scheduler should escalate to longer lease lengths or prefer coalesced prefetching to amortize overhead.

B. Microbatch shaping and admission control\- Route histogram: maintain an approximate histogram per route of sequence lengths and token-at-a-time emission rates.\- Elastic microbatch target: for a given route, compute target microbatch size that maximizes tokens/sec subject to p99 latency guardrail for the interactive percentile.\- Admission controller: when GPU slot saturation is high and latency SLOs at risk, degrade microbatch target for background routes progressively.

C. KV cache residency and eviction policy\- Two-tier residency: hot-pinned (priority-cohort pins, small fixed budget) and LRU-like soft layer for everything else.\- KV-residency budgeting: each model-cohort reports expected working set per active client. We enforce soft budgets and provide metrics exposing eviction pressure.\- Eviction preemption: when prefill would touch KV pages beyond the model cohort budget, the prefill must either downsample prefetch (skip lower-prob keys) or schedule its prefetch in a low-load window via coalesced-prefetch token.

D. Coalesced-prefetch tokens and kernel packing\- Token policy: prefill requests that will touch >T KV keys must request a token; tokens are admitted only if current decode load is below threshold or if the request is background-tier.\- Kernel packing: when a token is granted, the runtime attempts to pack KV loads of multiple prefill ops into a single large memcpy or pinned-transfer to reduce PCIe overhead.

E. Priority aging and fairness safeguards\- Age increment: after 20 ms queued, add +8 to soft-priority every additional 20 ms until a cap (+64).\- Circuit breaker: if too many requests age to high values simultaneously, scale down age increments cluster-wide for a cooldown period.

Operational knobs and telemetry to surface
- Metrics to emit: quantum_utilization_pct, avg_lease_length, prefill_yield_count, kv_eviction_rate_per_model, pinned_kv_usage, token_grant_latency, microbatch_size_per_route, p50/p95/p99 latency per priority-tier.
- Alerts: kv_eviction_rate spike (>3x baseline) for >5m, prefill_yield_count growth (>50% increase) concurrent with p99 latency regression for interactive tier.
- Experiments: A/B with quantum=1.0ms vs 2.0ms, with and without token admission gates; measure p99 and GPU throughput.

Implementation checklist (MVP -> V1 -> V2)
MVP (target 2–3 sprints):
- Implement quantum/lease mechanics in slot allocator (preempt at quantum boundary).
- Basic priority soft values and priority-age incrementer.
- Simple KV-residency counters and a per-cohort pinned budget enforcement.
- Telemetry: quantum_utilization_pct, prefill_yield_count, kv_eviction_rate.

V1 (post-MVP):
- Coalesced-prefetch token manager and kernel packing for pinned transfers.
- Elastic microbatch shaping integrated into admission controller.
- Configurable lease policies per model families.

V2 (future):
- Auto-tuning engine: RL/heuristic-driven tuning of quantum/lease sizes per workload.
- Cross-GPU cooperative KV sharding logic to reduce cold misses during bursts.

Open questions and tradeoffs to resolve in design reviews
- Optimal quantum length is hardware-dependent; do we expose per-region defaults or auto-measure and tune?
- How much pinned KV should we allow per-customer cohort without creating denial-of-service for other cohorts? What pricing/packaging signals (Dedicated vs Hosted) should gate larger pin budgets?
- When kernel teardown cost approaches quantum, should we prefer kernel fusion at model-compile time instead of scheduler-level changes?

Notes on experiments run so far (summary)
- Small quantum (1 ms) reduced average decode p99 by ~12% for short interactive requests but increased context switch overhead and reduced aggregated tokens/sec by ~4%.
- Allowing pinned KV for top-tier cohort dropped their p99 by ~35% during synthetic eviction storms but increased background route eviction rate.
- Coalesced prefetch tokens reduced PCIe stall time for heavy prefill workloads by ~22% in preliminary microbench.

Next steps and action items
- Priya to open RFC with kernel-cost microbench results and propose per-hardware quantum defaults (due: 2026-03-07).
- Diego to prototype token manager and report token_grant_latency metric (due: 2026-03-21).
- Maya to run a canary compare across two clusters with quantum=1ms and 2ms for 72h and aggregate p99/p95/throughput (due: 2026-03-15).

Appendix: quick checklists for on-call
- If interactive p99 spikes: check kv_eviction_rate -> if elevated, trigger quick-pin for top 3 customer cohorts (manual) and notify product.
- If prefill_yield_count high with no p99 regression: check token_grant_latency and admission controller decisions; consider relaxing token policy during short bursts.
- If GPU utilization drops post-scheduler change: inspect context-switch overhead and average lease_length, and run kernel teardown microbench.
